title: Kernel & DSA language, threading and IPC architecture

record.decision_title: D2: Kernel and DSA language, threading and IPC design. Decision: TypeScript kernel in a dedicated kernel Web Worker, a pool of nested executor workers, a hand-written {id, call, args} protocol with Valibot schemas
context_constraints_ranked: 1. Main-thread responsiveness (boundary 2, PROC-05, WM-03). The main thread only renders and dispatches. p95 frame must be <=16.7 ms with a CPU-bound job and 10 windows open, OS code must cause no long task over 50 ms, and the kernel may use at most about 4 ms of main-thread time per frame.

2. Typed syscall boundary (boundary 1, SYS-01, AGT-01/02). Every app, built-in ones included, talks to the kernel only with {id, call, args} -> {id, ok, value|errno}. The kernel checks permissions on every call. Agent tools are typed syscalls described by JSON Schema, and nothing is ever eval'd.

3. Hand-written DSA with provable complexity (s10). The heap, trie, tree, DAG with topological sort, and LRU list are written by the team, each in its own module under dsa/ with tests and a micro-benchmark. Budgets: SYS-03 p95 <=1 ms over >=10k entries; PROC-02 O(log n) push, pop and changePriority; MEM-02 O(1) touch and evict.
4. Testability. CI must report >=85% coverage on dsa/, kernel/ and vfs/ (>=70% overall) on every PR, plus property tests and integration tests for concurrency and kill paths.

5. Team skills and defensibility. Five BSCS students who know JS/TS, 18 weeks, Phase 2 due in week 7. Every member must defend every decision in the viva, and a decision only one person can explain counts as undefended.

6. Memory subsystem (MEM-01/03/05/06). A 5 MB page-in needs p95 <=300 ms locally. The accounting model has to be validated with performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory, which only works when the page is cross-origin isolated (COOP/COEP headers).
7. Boot budget (BOOT-10). Warm boot <=1.5 s and cold boot <=3.0 s to an interactive desktop on the modest lab machine, so every KB and every instantiate in the kernel path counts.

8. Robustness (PROC-05/07/09). Runaway processes are force-killed with worker.terminate() and the pool respawns. Kill frees fds and locks and re-parents children to init. The system must hold >=256 concurrent processes.
9. Offline and single local writer (OFF-01/02). The kernel runs fully from local state, and only one kernel may write the shared IndexedDB/OPFS store at a time, even when several tabs are open.

options.name: A. TypeScript kernel in a dedicated kernel worker (recommended)
options.current_version: TypeScript 7.0.2 (GA 2026-07-08; npm latest 2026-09); Chrome 153 stable Dedicated/nested Workers
options.summary: The kernel core (process table, scheduler, memory manager/pager, VFS, service manager, syscall dispatcher, sync client) runs in one dedicated module worker. That worker spawns the executor pool as nested dedicated workers. The main thread keeps only the compositor/WM, the app views and a small message router. App processes run as generator programs on executors. Syscalls go straight from each executor to the kernel over a MessagePort, so they never touch the main thread.
options.status_notes: The TS 7 native compiler has no programmatic API until 7.1 (beta planned for Oct 2026). Until then typescript-eslint runs on @typescript/typescript6 6.0.2.

options.name: B. TypeScript kernel on the main thread (spec reference layout)
options.summary: This is Figure 8.1 as drawn. The kernel lives on the main thread next to the compositor and keeps within 4 ms per frame, and only process slices run on workers. It is the simplest to debug (one thread, direct access to the compositor), but every syscall and every kernel computation queues behind rendering.
options.status_notes: The runner-up. Because the kernel core is transport-agnostic, this layout can be restored cheaply if we reverse the decision.

options.name: C. TypeScript kernel in a SharedWorker (one kernel for all tabs)
options.summary: One kernel is shared by every tab of the origin, which gives true multi-tab consistency and a single WebSocket.
options.status_notes: Measured in Chrome 153 with the same COOP/COEP headers: no Worker constructor (so it cannot own the executor pool), no createSyncAccessHandle, crossOriginIsolated=false and no SharedArrayBuffer. MDN lists SharedWorker as Baseline only since May 2026.

options.name: D. Rust -> WASM kernel core and DSA (wasm-bindgen) in a kernel worker
options.current_version: wasm-bindgen 0.2.128 (2026-09-04); wasm-pack 0.15.0 (2026-05-15, now under the wasm-bindgen org)
options.summary: Same placement as A, but the heap, LRU, trie, inode tree and permission logic are written in Rust and compiled to WASM. PCBs, strings and UI stay in TypeScript. The structures would still be hand-written, with no priority-queue or lru crates.
options.status_notes: The Rust project sunset the rustwasm GitHub org in July 2025. wasm-bindgen moved to its own org and is actively released. No team member is assumed to know Rust.

options.name: E. Go (TinyGo) -> WASM kernel (expected to lose)
options.current_version: Go 1.27.1 is latest (we measured with the locally installed Go 1.22.2 syscall/js); TinyGo v0.42.0 (2026-09-01)
options.summary: Kernel and DSA written in Go with goroutines, exported to JS through syscall/js (or go:wasmexport).
options.status_notes: Measured: a 50-line heap compiles to 1.56 MB of WASM (456 KB gzip), takes 130-208 ms to instantiate, costs 20-26 us per JS->Go call and 30-70 us per heap pop+push. In Go 1.24 the release notes describe go:wasmexport and reactor builds for wasip1.

options.name: F. AssemblyScript kernel and DSA in a kernel worker
options.summary: TypeScript-like syntax compiled to WASM. It gives near-WASM numeric speed without learning Rust.
options.status_notes: Still pre-1.0 with regular releases. Its semantics differ from TS (limited closures and unions, its own GC and runtime), and it has its own niche coverage and debug tooling.

evidence.claim: Pilot environment for all 'own pilot' rows: headless Google Chrome 153.0.8010.52 driven by playwright-core 1.63.0 on Linux, AMD Ryzen 5 7530U (6 cores / 12 threads), 31 GB RAM. Pages served with COOP same-origin and COEP require-corp; crossOriginIsolated was true and hardwareConcurrency 12. Results are from 2-3 repeated runs, so we report ranges. The pilot is indicative only: the team must repeat it on the Week-2 lab machine spec.
evidence.source: Own pilot harness: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-haseeb-raza-Desktop-Plotinium-OS/6bdb43c3-e62e-4f77-88ef-40bcd9948f85/scratchpad/kbench/run.mjs (+ www/main.js, kworker.js, appworker.js)

evidence.claim: Syscall round trip for a stat call with the result object, open-loop at one call every ~2-4 ms for 3 s (~730 calls). Kernel on the main thread: idle p50 85-140 us, p95 180-350 us. Same kernel while the main thread renders at 60 fps with 10 ms of work per frame: p50 1.8-2.0 ms, p95 9.3-9.5 ms, p99 ~10 ms. Kernel in a dedicated worker: idle p50 75-110 us, p95 140-340 us; under the same render load p50 65-75 us, p95 125-165 us.

Kernel work would break the main-thread budget. A du-style walk over a 100,000-node n-ary tree (Map children) took p50 4.2-6.9 ms and p95 7.0-14.8 ms, above the 4 ms per frame the reference allows for kernel work on the main thread.
Throughput is not the bottleneck: 10,000 pipelined stat syscalls ran at 78k-131k calls/s to a kernel worker and 66k-120k calls/s to a main-thread kernel (idle).

Binary heap, pop+push pair, steady state, n = 256 / 10^3 / 10^4 / 10^5. Idiomatic TS object heap with a Map index: 570-1,453 ns. changePriority: 86-422 ns. Struct-of-arrays TS heap (Float64Array keys, Int32Array pids): 92-198 ns. Hand-written WAT/WASM heap called from JS: 65-128 ns. An empty JS->WASM call costs 4.4-5.2 ns.
evidence.source: Own pilot, heap + wasm_noop_call_ns (heap.wat compiled with wabt 1.0.39)

evidence.claim: Trie complete(prefix, k=20) over path-like entries: p50 10-25 us and p95 30-50 us, flat from 10^3 to 10^5 entries. That is 20x under the SYS-03 1 ms budget. Just encoding the prefix and decoding 20 results through WASM linear memory costs p50 5 us and p95 5-15 us, so a WASM trie would pay about a third of the current total in marshalling alone. Timer resolution is 5 us in cross-origin-isolated pages (values were quantised to 5 us).
Page transfer, worker to worker, 5 MB ArrayBuffer: structured clone p50 6.9-9.3 ms, p95 9-14 ms. Transfer list: p50 0.05 ms, p95 0.85-1.2 ms.
SharedArrayBuffer control word: an Atomics.wait/notify ping-pong between two workers takes 8.0-9.4 us per round trip, and an Atomics.load pre-emption check at a yield point costs about 7.6-8.2 ns.

The kernel worker can own the pool. A nested dedicated worker spawned from the kernel worker is ready in p50 6.0-7.7 ms, p95 8.5-22 ms. worker.terminate() on a worker stuck in for(;;){} returns in about 0.01 ms, and a fresh worker replaces it.

Local swap in the kernel worker with an OPFS FileSystemSyncAccessHandle: 5 MB page-in including SHA-256 verification takes p50 24-31 ms and p95 35-56 ms, well inside the MEM-05 limit of 300 ms. Page-out (truncate, write, flush, hash) p95 is 59-194 ms.
createSyncAccessHandle() is only available in dedicated Web Workers.
A SharedWorker in Chrome 153 on the same COOP/COEP origin has no Worker constructor, no createSyncAccessHandle, crossOriginIsolated=false and no SharedArrayBuffer. navigator.locks is available.
evidence.source: Own pilot, sharedworker_caps; MDN SharedWorker page (Baseline since May 2026): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SharedWorker

evidence.claim: measureUserAgentSpecificMemory() requires cross-origin isolation (COOP+COEP) and has shipped since Chrome 89. It counts workers in the process. It resolves at the next GC, with a GC forced after about 20 s, so it suits calibrating the MEM-01 accounting model, not live accounting. In our headless pilot it took about 60 s to resolve.

COEP 'credentialless' is available from Chrome 96 and lets pages load cross-origin resources without CORP headers. Document-Isolation-Policy (Chrome 137+, desktop only) is a lighter alternative for getting crossOriginIsolated.

The Web Locks API works in workers and supports ifAvailable (fail immediately) and steal (force release). It has been Baseline widely available since March 2022, which makes it suitable for choosing one kernel tab.

Long Animation Frames (Chrome 123+) attribute scripts only on the main thread, not in workers. So a kernel in a worker cannot produce main-thread long tasks, and LoAF attribution can show that no long frame comes from OS code (PROC-05).

TypeScript 7.0, the Go-native compiler, went GA on 2026-07-08 and npm latest is 7.0.2. It ships without a stable programmatic API until 7.1, so typescript-eslint needs the @typescript/typescript6 compatibility package (6.0.2).

The Rust project sunset the rustwasm GitHub org in July 2025 and moved wasm-bindgen to a new org. wasm-bindgen 0.2.128 was released 2026-09-04 and wasm-pack 0.15.0 on 2026-05-15 under the wasm-bindgen org.

V8 still lists inlining across the JS-to-Wasm language boundary as future work (M137 speculative-optimisation post). JS->WASM calls stay cheap for numbers (about 5 ns measured), but strings and objects must be copied.

Go 1.22.2 with syscall/js: a 50-line heap compiles to 1,560,642 bytes of WASM (455,851 gzip), instantiates in 130-208 ms, costs 20-26 us per JS->Go call, and takes 30-70 us per heap pop+push. Go 1.24 added go:wasmexport and wasip1 reactor builds; the team could re-measure with Go 1.27 or TinyGo 0.42 if anyone argues for Go.

record.recommendation:
DECISION: Option A. The kernel and all of dsa/ are written in TypeScript (strict, TS 7.0.x). The kernel core runs in ONE dedicated module worker (kernel.worker.ts). That worker spawns a pool of nested executor workers, N = clamp(navigator.hardwareConcurrency - 2, 2, 8), plus one lazily started AI-runtime worker after the desktop is interactive. The main thread hosts only the compositor/WM (registry, z-order, focus, taskbar, pointer capture, transforms batched per requestAnimationFrame), the app views and a small router. It is budgeted at <=4 ms of OS script per frame and checked with Long Animation Frames attribution.

WHY. (1) In our Chrome 153 pilot, a main-thread kernel's syscall p95 grew from 0.2-0.35 ms to 9.4 ms as soon as the UI did 10 ms of work per frame. The worker kernel stayed at 0.13-0.17 ms p95. Kernel bookkeeping such as a 100k-node walk (7-15 ms p95) would otherwise break the 4 ms/frame rule. (2) Only a dedicated worker has OPFS sync access handles, Atomics.wait and the ability to own and terminate nested workers. In the pilot, a 5 MB page-in with SHA-256 verification took 35-56 ms p95, against the 300 ms MEM-05 limit. (3) WASM makes a heap op 5-10x faster in isolation (65-128 ns vs 570-1,453 ns), but one IPC hop costs 65-110 us and every structure already beats its budget by 20x or more in TS. The costs are real by contrast: a second coverage toolchain, weaker debugging, string marshalling (5-15 us per trie completion) and a language the team does not know. (4) A SharedWorker kernel cannot spawn workers, use sync OPFS or get cross-origin isolation (measured in Chrome 153).

PROCESS MODEL. Every program is a generator ('function*'). yield is either a syscall request or a cheap yield point. An executor runs one quantum per dispatch: 5, 10 or 20 ms for the interactive, normal and background bands, configurable for PROC-03. It stops early when a SharedArrayBuffer pre-empt flag is set, then reports {pid, cpuMs, status}. The kernel keeps a watchdog: past the hard limit it sets a kill flag, waits 100 ms, then calls worker.terminate(), respawns the executor (about 6-8 ms) and records exit code 137 for the runaway. CPU hogs are moved to executors of their own so a forced kill takes no other process with it. State stays on its home executor; it moves only through the pager (page-out, then page-in elsewhere).

IPC. A hand-written protocol, not Comlink: requests {id, call, args}, replies {id, ok:true, value} or {id, ok:false, errno}. The caller's identity comes from the executor port and the kernel's resident table, never from the message. Every call is validated with a Valibot schema, permission-checked against the PCB's uid/gid and appended to the audit ring buffer. Payloads over 64 KB are transferred, not cloned (5 MB: 0.05 ms vs 9 ms). SharedArrayBuffer is used only for a 32-byte control block per executor (pre-empt/kill flag, running pid, heartbeat, slice sequence), never for data. COOP same-origin plus COEP credentialless are set everywhere, including on Service-Worker-served offline navigations. If the page is not cross-origin isolated, the OS degrades to message-based pre-emption.

SCHEMAS. Valibot 1.5 plus @valibot/to-json-schema 1.8. One schema per syscall. Agent tools are a typed subset of these schemas, exported at build time as JSON Schema for the server-side LLM gateway. Valibot is 2.5 KB gzip, uses no eval (compatible with a strict script-src 'self' CSP) and validates in about 0.9 us, roughly 1% of one IPC hop.

HASH TABLE. Yes, write one for distinction credit: dsa/hashtable/PidTable.ts (open addressing, linear probing, Fibonacci hashing, backward-shift deletion, load factor <=0.5, doubling). It backs the process table (PROC-01) and is differential-tested against Map with fast-check. Every other registry uses the built-in Map.

MULTI-TAB. Only one tab may run the kernel. navigator.locks.request('plotinium:kernel', {ifAvailable:true}) elects it. A second tab shows 'Plotinium is running in another tab: use here', and a BroadcastChannel message asks the leader to shut down gracefully first.

IF SKILLS DIFFER. If two or more members are already fluent in Rust, keep this design and allow at most one numeric hot module (heap or LRU) in Rust->WASM behind the same TS interface. Do that only if its micro-benchmark misses budget, and add cargo-llvm-cov to CI so coverage still applies.
record.runner_up: Option B, the TypeScript kernel on the main thread (the spec's reference layout), scored 3.75 against A's 4.70. It wins only on debuggability, and it loses heavily on syscall latency under UI load (measured p95 9.4 ms vs 0.13-0.17 ms) and on capabilities (no OPFS sync handles, no Atomics.wait). Switching back is cheap because the kernel core is transport-agnostic: kernel/core has no self, document or Worker references, and a host adapter (worker.ts, main.ts or loopback.ts for tests) binds it to ports. Moving it to the main thread would mean changing the host file plus chunking long kernel operations.
record.chat_reason: Write the kernel and all data structures in TypeScript, and run the kernel in its own Web Worker instead of on the main thread. In our Chrome 153 test, system calls to a main-thread kernel took up to 9.4 ms while the UI was busy, against about 0.15 ms from a worker kernel. Rust/WASM did make a heap operation 5-10x faster, but that gain is under 1 microsecond against a 65-110 microsecond message hop, and it would cost us coverage tooling, easy debugging and time spent learning a new language. Messages use a small hand-written {id, call, args} protocol checked by Valibot schemas, big buffers are transferred instead of copied, and a tiny shared-memory flag lets the kernel pre-empt a running process.
record.gave_up: 1. WASM's raw numeric speed: a 5-10x faster heap in micro-benchmarks, and Rust's memory-safety story. 2. The simplicity of a single-threaded kernel. Window syscalls now take two hops (app -> kernel -> compositor), and the kernel has to mirror window ownership (wid -> pid) while the compositor owns geometry, z-order and focus. 3. A true multi-tab kernel. Only one tab runs Plotinium at a time, and other tabs offer a takeover. 4. Zod's familiarity and larger ecosystem, and Comlink's convenience (proxied objects, no envelope code). 5. Strong isolation between processes that share an executor. JS gives no memory isolation inside one worker, so untrusted or CPU-heavy code gets an executor of its own, and real third-party app isolation (sandboxed iframes) is deferred to future work. 6. Freedom from cross-origin-isolation headaches. We accept COOP/COEP on every response, including cached offline ones.

risks.risk: Cross-thread bugs between the compositor and the kernel's window-ownership mirror: stale focus, windows left behind after kill (WM-01..06, PROC-07).
risks.mitigation: Single-authority rule: the compositor owns geometry, z-order and focus; the kernel owns wid->pid ownership and lifecycle. Every cross-thread message carries a sequence number and correlation ID and is traced in the kernel log ring buffer. A fast-check model test fires random spawn, kill, close and focus sequences and checks that both sides agree.

risks.risk: Cross-origin isolation gets lost: headers missing from Service-Worker-cached responses offline, a CDN resource blocked, or the examiners' proxy stripping headers.
risks.mitigation: Use COEP credentialless, so the model CDN needs no CORP. The Service Worker stores the whole Response and re-emits COOP/COEP on navigations. The POST boot stage logs crossOriginIsolated, and an e2e test checks it both online and on offline boot. If isolation is missing, the SAB control block is switched off, pre-emption falls back to messages, and MEM calibration is marked unavailable in bootlog. Document-Isolation-Policy (Chrome 137+ desktop) is a fallback.

risks.risk: worker.terminate() on a shared executor also kills co-resident processes.
risks.mitigation: Placement policy: a process that overruns its quantum twice is moved to its own executor, and AI jobs have a dedicated worker. Before termination, co-residents with a clean swap copy are restored on the respawned executor; any others get exit 137 with reason 'collateral', logged and explained in the defence.

risks.risk: The single kernel worker becomes a bottleneck with 256 processes, or a long bulk operation (rm -r on 1,000 nodes) blocks other syscalls.
risks.mitigation: Measured capacity is 78k-131k simple syscalls/s. Heavy user-space commands (find, grep, du) run in executors and call syscalls. Bulk kernel operations are resumable generators that yield every 2 ms; only the final commit is non-pre-emptible. The kernel's busy fraction is tracked and shown in top.

risks.risk: The generator programming model is unfamiliar, and a missing yield in a loop causes runaway slices.
risks.mitigation: Provide a tiny proc runtime (yield* sys.read(...), yield ctx.tick) with examples and an ESLint rule that flags loops with no yield inside function* in apps/ and bin/. The watchdog plus terminate is the safety net, and each slice overrun is logged with its pid.

risks.risk: Code that only runs in workers is not counted toward the 85% coverage target.
risks.mitigation: Keep kernel/core and dsa/ free of DOM and worker globals, enforced with ESLint no-restricted-globals, and test them in Node through a loopback transport with V8 coverage. The worker host shims stay under 50 lines and are covered by Vitest browser-mode or Playwright integration tests.

risks.risk: TypeScript 7 tooling gaps: no programmatic API until 7.1 (beta around October 2026).
risks.mitigation: Use tsc 7.0.x for type-checking and @typescript/typescript6 6.0.2 for typescript-eslint. Vite and Vitest transpile without tsc. Pin exact versions at the week-4 freeze; moving to 7.1 requires a new decision record.

risks.risk: Micro-benchmark noise: timers in cross-origin-isolated pages have 5 us resolution, and CPU frequency scaling makes idle latency look worse than loaded latency.
risks.mitigation: Time batches of N operations and divide. Report p50 and p95 over at least 1,000 runs, discard warm-up, fix seeds, and run on the published lab-spec machine plus a 4x CPU-throttled CDP profile.

risks.risk: Valibot's JSON Schema output does not match the LLM provider's accepted tool-schema subset (strict mode, additionalProperties).
risks.mitigation: A CI contract test generates every tool schema and validates it against the provider's rules. Tool schemas are generated at build time on the server side only. The fallback is Zod 4 toJSONSchema in the shared abi/ package, a swap limited to that one package.

record.reversal_trigger:
Revisit this decision if any of the following is measured on the published lab-spec machine in Chrome stable:

(1) Under the PROC-05 stress (10 windows dragged plus a CPU-bound process), the kernel-worker syscall RTT p95 exceeds 2 ms, or the kernel worker is busy more than 50% of any 1 s window at 256 processes (PROC-09). Then split VFS and sync into a second worker first, and only after that consider option B.

(2) After a struct-of-arrays rewrite in TypeScript, a DSA benchmark still misses its budget: trie completion p95 >1 ms at 10^5 entries, heap push/pop p95 >5 us at 10^5, LRU touch/evict p95 >5 us at 10^5 pages, or scheduler dispatch overhead >50 us per decision at 256 processes. Then port only that numeric module to Rust->WASM behind the same interface.

(3) Window syscall round trips (app -> kernel -> compositor) exceed p95 16.7 ms, or the ownership-mirror model test finds divergence that cannot be fixed. Then move window ownership into a main-thread kernel shim.

(4) Cross-origin isolation cannot be kept on the production host or on offline boot. Then drop the SAB control block and use message-only pre-emption.

(5) Syscall-heavy tools such as find over 10k inodes spend more than 50% of their time in the IPC hop even with batched calls (readdirPlus). Then add a SharedArrayBuffer ring-buffer fast path for stat and readdir.

record.design_notes:
THREAD MAP
- Main thread:
  - compositor/WM, the single authority for geometry, z-order, focus and the taskbar
  - app view components
  - boot and login screens
  - kernel-link router
  - frame and LoAF monitor
  It never runs VFS, scheduler or pager logic.
- kernel.worker.ts, one dedicated module worker. It holds:
  - the syscall dispatcher, permission checks and audit ring buffer
  - the PCB table (own PidTable)
  - the scheduler (ready heap, timer/sleep heap, aging, RR by seq)
  - the memory manager (LRU list plus page tables; swap through OPFS sync handles and IndexedDB, remote swap over HTTPS)
  - the VFS (inode tree, dentry Maps, trie index updates, and one IndexedDB transaction per operation)
  - the service manager (DAG and Kahn levels)
  - the IPC bus, the sync client (the WebSocket lives here, since workers support it) and the outbox
- Executor pool: nested dedicated workers owned by the kernel, N = clamp(hardwareConcurrency - 2, 2, 8).
- ai.runtime worker: a separate executor class, started only after the desktop is interactive (BOOT-10). The indexer and predictor are ordinary PCBs with priority 32.
- The kernel core has no dependency on the thread it runs in. kernel/host/{worker,main,loopback}.ts bind ports; kernel/core imports none of self, document, Worker or indexedDB (ESLint no-restricted-globals).

ABI (kernel/abi, shared by the kernel, the executor runtime and the server gateway)
type Errno = 'ENOENT'|'EEXIST'|'ENOTDIR'|'EISDIR'|'ENOTEMPTY'|'EINVAL'|'EACCES'|'EPERM'|'ELOOP'|'EDQUOT'|'EBUSY'|'ENAMETOOLONG'|'ESRCH'|'EBADF'|'ENOSYS'|'EINTR'|'EAGAIN';
interface Req { id: number; pid: number; call: CallName; args: unknown }   // an executor forwards pid; the kernel checks it is resident on THAT executor's port
type Res = { id: number; ok: true; value: unknown } | { id: number; ok: false; errno: Errno; msg?: string };
const table = { stat: { schema: StatArgs, cls: 'fast', run: (p, a) => vfs.stat(p.cred, a.path, a) },
                unlink: { schema: UnlinkArgs, cls: 'bulk-nonpreemptive', run: ... }, ... } satisfies Record<CallName, Entry>;

Dispatch order for each call:
1. Look up the resident table for this port and pid; on failure return ESRCH.
2. Look up table[call]; if missing return ENOSYS.
3. v.safeParse(schema, args); on failure return EINVAL.
4. Permission check with PCB uid/gid.
5. audit.push({pid, uid, call, args, actor: agent? 'agent':'user'}).
6. Run the handler.
7. Reply.

Blocking calls (read on an empty pipe, a lock wait, a page fault) set PCB.state = BLOCKED and waitingOn; the kernel replies later. Payloads over 64 KB always go in the transfer list. Pipes are kernel ring buffers (extra DSA credit). Batched calls such as readdirPlus return stat together with names, so find needs fewer hops.

PROGRAM MODEL (bin/*.ts, apps/*/proc.ts)
export default function* wc(ctx: Ctx): Program {
  const fd = yield* ctx.sys.open(ctx.argv[1], 'r');
  let n = 0;
  for (;;) {
    const b = yield* ctx.sys.read(fd, 65536);
    if (!b.byteLength) break;
    for (const c of b) if (c === 10) n++;
    yield ctx.tick;
  }
  yield* ctx.sys.write(1, n + '\n');
  return 0;
}

EXECUTOR SLICE LOOP
function runSlice(pid, quantumMs, resume) {
  const P = resident.get(pid), end = performance.now() + quantumMs;
  let input = resume;
  for (;;) {
    const r = P.gen.next(input); input = undefined;
    if (r.done) return report(pid, 'exit', r.value);
    if (r.value !== TICK) { kport.postMessage(r.value); return report(pid, 'syscall', r.value.id); }
    Atomics.add(ctl, HB, 1);
    if (Atomics.load(ctl, PREEMPT) || performance.now() >= end) return report(pid, 'yield');
  }
}

A syscall ends the slice implicitly. For 'fast' calls the kernel replies with {type:'resume', pid, res, quantumLeft} straight away if peek() shows nothing with higher priority is READY, which is O(1). The result travels inside the dispatch or resume message on the executor's control port, so there is no ordering race between two ports.

Quanta: 5 ms for interactive (priority 0-9), 10 ms for normal (10-29), 20 ms for background (30-39); configurable. Heap key = effPrio * 2^32 + seq, stored in a Float64Array and exact below 2^53. Aging is changePriority through the index map, O(log n).

SAB CONTROL BLOCK (only when crossOriginIsolated)
Int32Array(8) per executor:
- [0] PREEMPT: 0 none, 1 yield, 2 kill
- [1] RUNNING_PID
- [2] HEARTBEAT
- [3] SLICE_SEQ
- [4..7] reserved (accounting)

The kernel sets PREEMPT=1 when a higher-priority process becomes READY and no executor is idle. Measured cost of the check is about 8 ns per yield point, and wake-up latency about 9 us.

WATCHDOG
Every 50 ms (setInterval is fine here; only boot progress must not be timer-driven) the kernel checks each running slice:
1. If elapsed > hardLimit (default max(20 * quantum, 250 ms)) and HEARTBEAT has not changed, set PREEMPT=2.
2. If there is still no report 100 ms later, call worker.terminate() and respawn the executor (measured p50 6-8 ms).
3. Mark the runaway TERMINATED with exit code 137, close its fds, release its locks, re-parent its children to pid 1 and tell the compositor to close its windows (PROC-07).
4. Restore co-resident processes from clean swap copies where possible; otherwise kill them with exit 137 and reason 'collateral'.

Mid-slice termination loses nothing in the kernel. Syscalls are atomic at call granularity, VFS operations commit in one IndexedDB transaction, and the kernel owns every fd and lock.

PAGING PATH
1. The memory manager calls executor.pageOut(pid, pageIds).
2. The executor serializes the pages with its codec into an ArrayBuffer and transfers it to the kernel (5 MB transferred in about 0.05 ms).
3. The kernel writes the OPFS sync handle and verifies SHA-256 with crypto.subtle.
4. Only then does it tell the executor to release the pages (MEM-03).

Page-in reverses the path and can target any executor, which is also how processes migrate. The accounting model is serialized bytes plus declared assets. It is calibrated offline against measureUserAgentSpecificMemory, which is slow (20-60 s), so it is never used in the live loop.

WINDOW SYSCALLS
Path: app -> kernel (checks that pid owns wid) -> compositor over the kernel-only port. The compositor accepts commands only from that port. Pointer drags stay local to the main thread (translate3d batched per requestAnimationFrame). Only the final geometry is sent to the kernel, for session restore (WM-06). Focus and minimise events flow to the kernel, which pins the focused process and makes minimised ones the first paging candidates.

Views talk to their process over a display MessageChannel (state snapshots and diffs out, input events in) that the kernel creates at sys.window.create. Before loading app code, the executor shadows indexedDB, caches, navigator.storage and Worker. This is defence in depth and does not replace the lint rules and the SYS-01 bypass test.

HASH TABLE (dsa/hashtable/PidTable.ts, distinction credit)
- Keys in an Int32Array, -1 means empty; values in an array.
- Capacity is a power of two; slot = (Math.imul(k, 0x9E3779B1) >>> shift) & mask.
- Linear probing; resize by doubling at load factor >0.5.
- Deletion uses backward shift, so there are no tombstones.
- Tests: edge cases (empty, one element, reinsert after delete, wrap-around cluster), a fast-check differential test against Map, and a benchmark of get/set/delete from 10^3 to 10^5.
- Used by the process table. Everything else uses Map/Set, as the spec allows.

HEADERS
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless go on every HTML and JS response: Vite server.headers, the production proxy (Caddy/nginx), and Service-Worker-served navigations, which re-emit the headers from the cached Response. CSP: script-src 'self', worker-src 'self', no 'unsafe-eval'. Valibot needs no eval.

MULTI-TAB
In the kernel worker at the POST stage:
1. Call navigator.locks.request('plotinium:kernel', {ifAvailable:true}, () => new Promise(never)).
2. If the lock is null, the tab shows a takeover screen. BroadcastChannel('plotinium:ctl') asks the leader to shut down gracefully (flush dirty pages and the outbox, stop services in reverse topological order, release the lock).
3. {steal:true} is used only if the leader is unresponsive after 3 s.

REPO
kernel/{core,host,abi,runtime}, dsa/{heap,trie,tree,dag,lru,hashtable,ringbuffer}/{src,tests,bench}, wm/, vfs/, apps/, bin/, bench/spikes/kernel/.

spec_gaps: MEM-03/MEM-04 vs the generator process model: the record says 'Every program is a generator', that state moves only through the pager, and that co-resident processes are 'restored from clean swap copies'. A suspended JS generator cannot be serialized (structuredClone throws DataCloneError), yet MEM-03 requires page-out to serialize 'the state' and restore it byte-identical, and MEM-04 is verified by 'Close the tab, reopen it, restore the state'. The record needs an explicit process-state model: serializable state plus a re-creatable generator, page-out only at yield points, and a deterministic codec.

Boundary 1 on the main thread: app view components run in the same realm as the compositor and can reach indexedDB, localStorage and other windows' DOM. The record shadows globals only inside executors. It needs lint rules (no storage globals, no document queries outside the window's own root) for apps/*/view, a shadow root per window, and a SYS-01 bypass test that also covers view code.

AGT-08 (every agent syscall audited, viewable with 'ai log') and the s11 audit_log table: the record appends every call to an in-memory audit RING BUFFER, which overwrites old entries. Agent-originated calls need a durable audit row written in the same IndexedDB transaction as the operation and replicated to the server audit_log through the outbox.

DB-02 / fault injection on the client mirror: the risk mitigation says bulk kernel operations 'yield every 2 ms'. An IndexedDB transaction auto-commits once no requests are pending across a task boundary, and interleaved syscalls would see a half-applied in-memory tree. rm -r, mv, cp -r and chmod -R must therefore be two-phase: a pre-emptible plan phase under an in-kernel subtree lock with no transaction open, then a non-pre-emptible apply phase that mutates memory and issues one IDB transaction with no await on crypto or network inside it, plus an undo log so the in-memory tree reverts if the transaction aborts.

Security model / AGT-04: the executor forwards the pid and the kernel only checks that the pid is resident on that port. Processes that share an executor share a JS realm, so a process can forge a co-resident process's pid. Executors must be partitioned by credential (uid, and agent vs user) or the threat model must say explicitly that only first-party code runs.

BOOT-01 POST and OFF-05: persist(), Service Worker registration and updates, and measureUserAgentSpecificMemory are Window-only in Chrome, so part of POST has to stay on the main thread. The record places POST in the kernel worker.

BOOT-10: the kernel-worker spawn plus executor-pool spawn on the boot critical path was never measured, and C7 gives A a 5 while penalising only WASM instantiate. Spawn one executor at boot and the rest after the desktop is interactive, and measure time-to-kernel-ready on the lab machine.

PROC-05/WM-03 input latency: the display MessageChannel goes from view to process directly and bypasses the kernel, so the kernel cannot pre-empt a background slice when input arrives. The input then waits up to one quantum (20 ms), or until the watchdog (≥350 ms) if a runaway shares the executor. Also, structured-clone deserialization of large kernel-to-view payloads costs main-thread time.
MEM-06 / DSA memory: C2 and reversal trigger (2) cover time only. There is no bytes-per-entry budget, although the pilot trie design needs about 493 MB at 10^5 entries.

Several tabs (spec §2 table, line 'Several tabs, devices and users can change the same data') and VFS-09 ('Two browsers, two users'): the record should state that two-user demos use two browsers, profiles or machines, because a second tab in the same profile gets the takeover screen.

Secure context: OPFS, Service Workers and SharedArrayBuffer all require a secure context. If examiners open the Docker bring-up at a plain-http LAN address rather than http://localhost, OPFS swap and the offline shell disappear, and the degrade path only covers losing SAB. The README and POST must say so.

The s14.2 row is 'Kernel and DSA language' (raw performance vs JS-WASM boundary, debugging, team skills). The record merges it with a thread-placement decision, so C1/C6/C8 (35%) do not discriminate between the language options at all. Present it as linked sub-decisions D2a (language) and D2b (placement/IPC), each with its own options and weights.
weaknesses: The weights do not look reverse-engineered in effect, but there is no proof that they were declared first. A scores ≥ every other option on 5 of 8 criteria and is at most 1 point behind on the other 3. I recomputed: under equal weights A=4.63, B=3.75, F=3.50, D=3.38, C=3.25, E=2.13, so A wins without the chosen weights. D beats A only under a pure-performance weighting (C1 30 / C2 50 / C7 20: D 4.8 vs A 4.5). Commit the criteria and weights in a git commit that predates the spike results, and include this sensitivity table.

Option B is partly scored as a strawman. C6=2 assumes a main-thread kernel cannot use OPFS sync handles, but the spec's reference layout already has a worker layer where swap I/O could run. C7 gives A the same 5 as B even though A adds a worker spawn to the boot path. Neither change alters the ranking, but examiners will press on both.

B's 9.4 ms p95 under load comes from a synthetic 10 ms busy loop per frame (about 60% main-thread utilisation), so the number is set by the load chosen. It demonstrates queueing, not realistic magnitude. The M1 prototype's real 10-window drag is the evidence that should go into STACK_DECISION.md.

The pilot ran with COEP require-corp and raw files and no bundler, while the recommendation uses COEP credentialless and Vite. I closed that gap: Vite 8.3.0 builds nested module workers (main -> kernel.worker -> executor.worker), and with COOP same-origin + COEP credentialless, crossOriginIsolated and SharedArrayBuffer are available in both the kernel and the nested executor, in dev and preview (Chrome 153; .../scratchpad/exam/vt/run.mjs). The team should reproduce this in M7.

The pilot ran on a 12-thread Ryzen with 31 GB of RAM. On a 4-thread lab machine the pool is main + kernel + 2 executors + the AI worker (plus onnxruntime-web threads), which oversubscribes the cores. The reversal trigger covers this, but none of the evidence does yet.

The idiomatic Map-per-node DSA style that the record benchmarks is memory-infeasible at 10^5 entries (trie: 493 MB). The record prefers struct-of-arrays only for the heap. The same argument ('TS with typed arrays is enough, no WASM needed') should be applied and measured for the trie and the LRU.

The toolchain runs on very fresh releases at freeze time: TS 7.0.2 with no API plus a TS6 alias, Vitest 5.0.1 (5.0.0 released 2026-09-03), Vite 8.3.0. Two compilers can disagree on type errors. Declare which one is the CI gate and pin exact versions.

Trie key design is not specified. If the trie indexes full paths, one 'mv' of a large directory means O(subtree × path length) re-indexing, which works against SYS-03's 'updated incrementally'. Index basenames or per-directory entries instead.

The generator/executor model moves every built-in app's logic (Editor, Files, Task Manager) into an executor behind a state-diff display protocol. That is a large Phase-2 (week 7) engineering load for the UI owner, and the record gives no estimate. Say explicitly which UI-local state (for example, the editor buffer before save) may stay in the view without breaching boundary 1.
examiner_review.amended_recommendation:
DECISION (upheld with changes): Option A. The kernel and all of dsa/ are written in strict TypeScript. The kernel core runs in ONE dedicated module worker (kernel.worker.ts), which owns a pool of nested executor workers, N = clamp(navigator.hardwareConcurrency - 2, 2, 8). Only one executor starts during boot; the others start after the desktop is interactive, and so does the AI-runtime worker (BOOT-10). The main thread hosts the compositor/WM (registry, z-order, focus, taskbar, pointer capture, translate3d batched per requestAnimationFrame), the app views and a small router. It also makes the platform calls a dedicated worker cannot make, and forwards the results to the kernel: navigator.storage.persist() at POST, Service Worker registration and 'restart to update' (OFF-05), and performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory() for MEM-01 calibration (in CI, run Chrome with --enable-blink-features=ForceEagerMeasureMemory, which resolves in about 20 ms). Main-thread OS script is budgeted at 4 ms or less per frame and checked with Long Animation Frames attribution. Payloads from the kernel to views are paginated or sent as transferables, because structured-clone deserialization is paid on the main thread. In STACK_DECISION.md this is presented as two linked records: D2a, language (TS vs Rust->WASM vs AssemblyScript vs Go), and D2b, placement and IPC (main thread vs dedicated worker vs SharedWorker).

TOOLCHAIN (corrected). devDependencies: "typescript": "npm:@typescript/typescript6@6.0.2" (the TS6 API, used by typescript-eslint 8.70.x, whose peer range is typescript <6.1.0, by editors, and by any template checker D1 needs) and "@typescript/native": "npm:typescript@7.0.2" (the native tsc). CI's type-check gate is TS 7 'tsc --noEmit'. tsconfig avoids the options removed in 7.0 (baseUrl, moduleResolution node10, target es5). Pin exact versions of valibot 1.5.0, @valibot/to-json-schema 1.8.0, vite 8.3.0, vitest, @vitest/coverage-v8 and @vitest/browser-playwright 5.0.1, fast-check 4.10.2, tinybench 6.2.0 and @playwright/test 1.63.0 (all confirmed as npm latest on 2026-09-23). Moving to TS 7.1 (stable 2026-11-24) needs a new record.

WHY. (1) Pilot on Chrome 153: a main-thread kernel's syscall p95 rose to 9.4 ms under 10 ms of render work per frame, while the worker kernel stayed at 0.13-0.17 ms. A 100k-node walk (7-15 ms p95) would break the 4 ms/frame rule. (2) Only a dedicated worker has OPFS sync access handles, Atomics.wait and the ability to own and terminate nested workers. A 5 MB page-in with SHA-256 verification took 35-56 ms p95, against the 300 ms limit. Vite 8.3 builds nested module workers, and with COOP same-origin plus COEP credentialless both the kernel and the executors are crossOriginIsolated with SharedArrayBuffer (examiner re-check). (3) WASM makes a heap operation faster in isolation (65-128 ns, against 92-198 ns for the struct-of-arrays TS heap), but one IPC hop costs 65-110 us, TS already meets every time budget by 20x or more, and WASM would add a second coverage toolchain, weaker debugging, string marshalling (5-15 us per trie completion) and a new language. (4) A SharedWorker cannot spawn workers, use sync OPFS or become cross-origin isolated.

DSA LAYOUT RULE. Large structures use struct-of-arrays typed-array layouts written from first principles: the trie (left-child/right-sibling or radix), the LRU list, the ready heap and the page tables. The pilot's Map-per-node trie needs 493 MB at 10^5 path entries (56 MB at 10^4). A TS typed-array trie holds the same data in 24 MB with completion p95 of 34 us. The trie indexes basenames or per-directory entries rather than full paths, so an mv of a directory stays an incremental update. Every dsa/ benchmark reports bytes per entry next to ns per op.

PROCESS MODEL (amended). A program is { init(argv) -> state, *run(ctx, state) }. Everything a process must keep lives in the serializable state or in ctx.mem segments, because generator objects cannot be serialized. Page-out happens only at a yield point: the state is encoded with a deterministic codec, SHA-256 is computed and verified after the write, and then the generator and state are dropped. Page-in rebuilds the generator with run(ctx, restoredState), on any executor. This is what makes MEM-03 byte-identical restore, MEM-04 restore from a new browser session, migration, and restore after collateral termination possible. Short-lived commands are not checkpointable, are never paged, and on collateral termination exit with 137 and the reason 'collateral'. Quanta are 5, 10 and 20 ms for the interactive, normal and background bands (configurable). A SharedArrayBuffer pre-empt flag is checked at yield points (about 8 ns). The watchdog sets the kill flag, waits 100 ms, then calls worker.terminate() and respawns the executor (6-8 ms), and a process that overruns twice gets an executor of its own. Placement: processes with different uids, and agent processes versus user processes, never share an executor, because processes in the same realm could forge each other's pid. The focused process is placed on the least-loaded executor. When input reaches a view's display channel, a flag is also set in the kernel's SAB, so a background slice on that executor is pre-empted at its next yield point.

BULK OPERATIONS. rm -r, cp -r, mv, batch rename and chmod/chown -R run in two phases. Phase 1 can be pre-empted and yields every 2 ms: it takes an in-kernel subtree lock (conflicting syscalls queue or get EBUSY), checks permissions and quota, hashes content and builds the plan and an undo log. No IndexedDB transaction is open during this phase. Phase 2 cannot be pre-empted: it applies the in-memory mutation and ONE readwrite IndexedDB transaction across all affected stores, issuing only IDB requests and never awaiting crypto or the network (IndexedDB auto-commits once nothing is pending). If the transaction aborts, the undo log reverts the in-memory tree. The fault-injection hook lives inside both phases.

IPC. A hand-written {id, call, args} -> {id, ok, value | errno} protocol, not Comlink. For each call the kernel checks residency (ESRCH), looks up the call (ENOSYS), validates it with Valibot (EINVAL), checks permissions against the PCB's uid/gid, audits it and runs it. Agent-originated calls are audited durably: the row is written in the same IDB transaction as the operation and queued in the outbox for the server's audit_log (AGT-08). The ring buffer holds only the in-memory kernel log. Payloads over 64 KB are transferred rather than cloned. SharedArrayBuffer is used only for the 32-byte control block per executor. Every HTML and JS response carries COOP same-origin and COEP credentialless, including navigations served by the Service Worker. The page must be served from a secure context (https, or http://localhost for the Docker bring-up), and POST logs isSecureContext and crossOriginIsolated. Without isolation, pre-emption falls back to messages; without a secure context, swap falls back to IndexedDB only and bootlog says so.

SCHEMAS. Valibot 1.5, one schema per syscall. Agent tool schemas are exported to JSON Schema at build time, on the server side only. A CI contract test checks them against the provider dialect chosen in D8; the fallback is Zod 4 toJSONSchema, confined to the abi/ package.

HASH TABLE. dsa/hashtable/PidTable.ts, for distinction credit: open addressing with linear probing, Fibonacci hashing, backward-shift deletion and load factor 0.5 or less. It is differential-tested against Map with fast-check and backs the process table (PROC-01).

MULTI-TAB. navigator.locks 'plotinium:kernel' with ifAvailable elects one kernel tab. A second tab offers takeover, with a graceful shutdown over BroadcastChannel and steal only after 3 s. Two-user demos (VFS-09 'two browsers, two users') use separate browsers, profiles or machines. Several local users share one kernel through login and su.

CHROME CADENCE. Chrome now ships stable every two weeks (154 on 2026-09-22). Nightly CI runs the capability and performance suite on Chrome stable and beta, and the spike is re-run on the stable that is current at each gate.

IF SKILLS DIFFER. If two or more members are fluent in Rust, keep this design and allow at most one numeric module in Rust->WASM behind the same TS interface. Do this only if its struct-of-arrays TS benchmark misses its time or memory budget, and add cargo-llvm-cov to CI.

ADDED REVERSAL TRIGGERS, on top of the original five. (6) After the struct-of-arrays rewrite, any dsa/ structure exceeds 32 MB at 10^5 entries: port that module only. (7) A new Chrome stable removes or regresses nested workers, SAB in workers or sync access handles: fall back to message pre-emption or IndexedDB swap, and re-open D2b. (8) Two-phase bulk operations cannot pass fault injection with a single IndexedDB transaction: re-open D2b together with the client-storage decision.

EVIDENCE HYGIENE. Rename option E to 'Go (gc, syscall/js)' or re-measure it with TinyGo 0.42 or Go 1.27.
examiner_review.amended_chat_reason: Keep the decision: write the kernel and every data structure in TypeScript, and run the kernel in its own Web Worker. In our test, system calls to a main-thread kernel took up to 9.4 ms while the UI was busy, against about 0.15 ms from a worker kernel. Rust/WASM only saves nanoseconds against a message hop of about 100 microseconds, and it would cost us coverage tooling, debugging and time learning a new language. The review found fixes to make before the defence. Install TypeScript 7 under an alias so ESLint keeps working. Use compact typed-array layouts for big structures: the prototype trie needs about 490 MB at 100k entries, a typed-array one needs 24 MB. Store each process's state explicitly so it can be paged out and restored, because a generator cannot be saved. Do bulk file operations in two phases so they stay atomic. Keep a few browser calls on the main thread, because a worker cannot make them. Retest on each new Chrome, which now ships every two weeks.

defence_qa.question: Figure 8.1 puts the kernel on the main thread. Why did you move it, and what did that cost you?
defence_qa.strong_answer: Section 8 calls the figure 'a reference, not a prescription' and asks us to keep three boundaries. Boundary 2 says the main thread only renders and dispatches. We measured both layouts in Chrome. With the UI busy, a main-thread kernel's syscall p95 was 9.4 ms against 0.13-0.17 ms in a worker, and a single 100k-node walk took 7-15 ms, over the 4 ms-per-frame budget. The cost is two hops for window syscalls and a wid-to-pid mirror between kernel and compositor. We control that with a single-authority rule (compositor owns geometry, z-order and focus; kernel owns ownership and lifecycle), sequence numbers, and a fast-check model test that kills and closes windows at random. Going back is cheap: kernel/core never touches self or document, so moving it means swapping one host adapter and chunking long operations.

defence_qa.question: Your processes are generators. How do you page one out and restore it byte-identical in a new browser session (MEM-03, MEM-04)?
defence_qa.strong_answer: We don't serialize the generator; a JS generator can't be serialized. A program is init(argv) -> state plus *run(ctx, state), and everything worth keeping lives in state or ctx.mem. We page out only at a yield point. The state is encoded with a deterministic codec, SHA-256 is computed, and it is written to OPFS or remote swap and read back to verify before anything is released. Page-in decodes, checks the hash, and calls run(ctx, state) again on any executor. Because of that, the same process restores after the tab is closed and reopened. Short-lived commands such as wc are never paged.

defence_qa.question: Rust->WASM made your heap 5-10x faster. Why isn't that decisive?
defence_qa.strong_answer: The gain is under a microsecond per operation: 65-128 ns in WASM against 92-198 ns for our struct-of-arrays TypeScript heap. One syscall hop costs 65-110 us, so it would not show in any user-facing latency. Every DSA budget is already met 20x over in TypeScript. The costs of WASM are measured too: 5-15 us of string marshalling per trie completion (a third of the whole completion), a second coverage toolchain, DWARF debugging documented only for C/C++, and a language none of us knows while Phase 2 is due in week 7. Our reversal trigger says that if one structure misses its time or memory budget after a struct-of-arrays rewrite, we port only that module to Rust behind the same interface.

defence_qa.question: A process on a shared executor hangs in for(;;){}. What exactly happens, and what does it cost the other processes on that worker?
defence_qa.strong_answer: The heartbeat in the SAB control block stops. Past the hard limit (at least 250 ms) the kernel sets PREEMPT=2, waits 100 ms, then calls worker.terminate() and respawns the executor in about 7 ms. The runaway gets exit code 137, and the kernel closes its fds, releases its locks, re-parents its children to init and closes its windows. The kernel owns all of that state, so nothing in the kernel is lost. Co-resident processes lose their un-yielded slice. Those with a clean checkpoint are restored on the new executor; the rest exit with 137 'collateral', and that is logged. We limit the damage in two ways: executors are split by uid and by agent versus user, and a process that overruns twice gets an executor of its own.

defence_qa.question: Your kernel yields every 2 ms during long operations. How is rm -r on 1,000 nodes still atomic when the fault hook fires at node 500?
defence_qa.strong_answer: It runs in two phases. Phase 1 can be pre-empted: it takes an in-kernel subtree lock so conflicting syscalls queue or get EBUSY, checks permissions and quota, and builds the plan and an undo log, with no IndexedDB transaction open. Phase 2 cannot be pre-empted: it applies the in-memory change and one readwrite IndexedDB transaction across inodes, dentries, quota and outbox, issuing only IDB requests so it can't auto-commit early. The hook throwing at node 500 aborts that transaction and the undo log restores the tree. The tree checksum, the orphan probe and the quota are all unchanged, and the server repeats the same thing in one Postgres transaction.

defence_qa.question: Your trie is flat at 30-50 us up to 10^5 entries. How much memory does it use, and does that fit a 256 MB budget on the lab machine?
defence_qa.strong_answer: In the pilot's Map-per-node form, no: 225 bytes per node, which is 56 MB at 10^4 entries and about 490 MB at 10^5. That is why the final trie is a struct-of-arrays left-child/right-sibling trie in typed arrays. It holds the same 10^5 entries in 24 MB with completion p95 of 34 us. Every dsa/ benchmark now reports bytes per entry next to ns per op, and one reversal trigger fires if any structure goes over 32 MB at 10^5 entries.
